questions.question_text: Of the following, which is the least common cause of malpractice claims against psychiatrists by patients?
questions.explanation: Sexual involvement with patients accounts for 6 percent of malpractice claims against psychiatrists and is the least common cause of malpractice litigation[cite: 21]. This fact does not, however, minimize its importance as a problem[cite: 22]. (It should be noted that the short statute of limitations for this particular offense may well discourage patients from pursuing litigation because they have not had sufficient time to reach a point of emotional readiness.) [cite: 23] Sexual intimacy with a patient is both illegal and unethical[cite: 23]. There are also serious legal and ethical questions about a psychotherapist's dating or marrying a patient even after discharging the patient from therapy[cite: 24]. Most psychiatrists believe in the adage "Once a patient, always a patient." [cite: 25] For other malpractice claims, the following figures are given: failure to manage suicide attempts, 21 percent [cite: 26]; failure to treat psychosis, 14 percent; and improper use of restraints, 7 percent[cite: 27]. Substance dependence accounts for about 10 percent of claims and refers to the patient's having developed a substance-related disorder as a result of a psychiatrist's not carefully monitoring the prescribing of potentially addicting drugs[cite: 28].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the basic elements of the insanity defense?

options.text: Presence of a defect of reason
Finding of incompetence to stand trial
Lack of knowledge of the nature of the act
Incapacity to refrain from the act

correct_answer.text: Finding of incompetence to stand trial

correct_answers.text: Finding of incompetence to stand trial

questions.explanation: No precise, generally accepted definition of legal insanity exists[cite: 30]. Tests of insanity have always been controversial and have undergone much modification and refinement over the years[cite: 30]. The insanity defense standard has four basic elements: 1. Presence of a mental disorder [cite: 31] 2. Presence of a defect of reason [cite: 32] 3. A lack of knowledge of the nature or wrongfulness of the act 4. An incapacity to refrain from the act [cite: 33] The insanity defense is one of the most controversial issues in American jurisprudence[cite: 34]. The presence of a mental disorder has remained the consistent core of the insanity defense [cite: 35]; the other elements have varied in importance over time[cite: 36]. The finding of incompetence to stand trial is unrelated to this defense[cite: 36]. Defendants with mental impairments who are found competent to stand trial may still seek acquittal on the claim of insanity, alleging that they were not criminally responsible for their actions at the time the offense was committed[cite: 37]. The term insanity is a legal construct, not a psychiatric diagnosis[cite: 38].

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old prisoner is found to have major depressive disorder. The correctional psychiatrist wants to start him on antidepressant therapy because of the severity of his disease. He was very often in solitary confinement for violent behavior with correctional staff. The prisoner refuses to take any medications, stating he does not want to complicate his life any more by having to take drugs every day. Correctional officers tell you it would be a security risk to have this prisoner out of his cell every day for treatment anyway. What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Do not give the prisoner antidepressants because he has the right to refuse.
Do not give the prisoner antidepressants because it is a security risk.
Do not give the prisoner antidepressants because it is not a medical emergency.
Give the prisoner antidepressants because he does not have the right to refuse.
Do nothing and observe the prisoner for worsening symptoms.

correct_answer.text: Give the prisoner antidepressants because he does not have the right to refuse.

correct_answers.text: Give the prisoner antidepressants because he does not have the right to refuse.

questions.explanation: The law and ethical analysis of informed consent and refusal inside corrections are complicated[cite: 40]. The legal rule is that inmates have the right to consent to care but do not necessarily have equally extensive rights to refuse care[cite: 41]. Complicating this issue is the reality that distinguishing between a refusal of care and a possible denial of care is often difficult[cite: 42]. An additional complication is the fact that other correctional staff may not want to offer appropriate psychiatric treatment for a variety of reasons (e.g.. security risks, cost, deservedness)[cite: 43]. Simultaneously, inmates can be insistent and manipulative and sometimes seek care for inappropriate reasons[cite: 44]. Despite these pressures from opposite poles, correctional psychiatric personnel must ensure that patients get appropriate care[cite: 45]. Medical autonomy means that nonmedical personnel cannot overrule the professional judgment of correctional psychiatrists regarding their patients' needs[cite: 46]. Medical autonomy means that only legitimate clinical decisions direct patient care, not patient wishes[cite: 47]. Correctional psychiatrists should be neutral in nonmedical matters[cite: 48]. Aligning with security staff costs them their rapport with their patients[cite: 48]. Alternatively, being inmate advocates for non-health-related issues would cost them their rapport with their correctional coworkers[cite: 49].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding juvenile detention centers is true?

options.text: Youth suicide in juvenile detention centers occur four times as often as youth suicide in the general population.
Suicide prevention guidelines are strictly enforced in juvenile detention centers.
Prevalence of mental illness in detention centers is extensively researched.
Juvenile detention centers are long-term facilities for juveniles convicted of crimes.
More than 80 percent of incarcerated boys meet the criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder.

correct_answer.text: Youth suicide in juvenile detention centers occur four times as often as youth suicide in the general population.

correct_answers.text: Youth suicide in juvenile detention centers occur four times as often as youth suicide in the general population.

questions.explanation: Youth suicide in juvenile detention and correctional facilities have been shown to occur four times more often than youth suicide in the general population[cite: 51]. Yet 75 percent of the nation's confined juveniles are in facilities that fail to conform to even the most basic suicide prevention guidelines[cite: 52]. Several studies note that 25 percent (not 80 percent) of incarcerated boys and 50 percent of incarcerated girls meet criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)[cite: 53]. Juvenile detention centers are short-term facilities that confine juveniles who are awaiting trial [cite: 54]; juvenile confinement facilities are long-term facilities (e.g., residential treatment centers and training schools) for the confinement of juveniles convicted of crimes[cite: 55]. Mental illness in detention centers has not been extensively researched[cite: 56].

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old white woman was admitted to a local hospital because of cocaine abuse and major depression with suicidal ideation. She had been referred to the hospital after being arrested for cocaine use. Which of the following is the most appropriate discharge plan for this patient?

options.text: Discharge to care of her family
Discharge to a psychiatric ward within a correctional facility
Discharge to a substance abuse detoxification center

correct_answer.text: Discharge to a psychiatric ward within a correctional facility

correct_answers.text: Discharge to a psychiatric ward within a correctional facility

questions.explanation: The most appropriate placement for this patient is in a psychiatric facility within a correctional facility[cite: 58]. Because she was arrested for cocaine use before her hospital referral, she still has charges pending against her and cannot be released to her home or the care of her family[cite: 59]. Although a substance abuse detoxification center may be helpful in the future, she first must have her legal situation dealt with[cite: 60]. Discharge to a local jail is inappropriate in this case as well because the local jail will not be able to adequately address her mental illness (major depression)[cite: 61].

questions.question_text: In the case above, the patient cut her wrists 4 days later. The most appropriate next step is

options.text: dismiss this act as it is manipulative
treat her as she has documented mental illness
complete examination by a mental health professional

correct_answer.text: complete examination by a mental health professional

correct_answers.text: complete examination by a mental health professional

questions.explanation: Because self-mutilation is hard to control, it is a serious challenge for correctional officials and psychiatric staff[cite: 63]. When self-mutilation is not the product of a mental disorder, mental health professionals often deny admission to the mental health unit[cite: 64]. This confuses correctional authorities who view such behavior as a sign of mental instability[cite: 65]. It is essential to have clear protocols for self-mutilation when it is (1) a psychiatric symptom, (2) a manipulative gesture to escape a dangerous situation, and (3) an effort to manipulate the system for personal gain[cite: 66]. This woman's documented history of major depressive disorder should alert correctional staff to the likelihood that cutting her wrists is a true suicide attempt[cite: 67]. She should have a complete evaluation by a psychiatrist to determine the extent of her current symptoms[cite: 68]. If this woman is indeed having an exacerbation of her symptoms of major depression, continuing to withhold medications and simply putting her on a one-on-one suicidal watch may not be enough and is neglectful[cite: 69]. However, a thorough evaluation should precede any treatment[cite: 70].

questions.question_text: In the case above, 2 days later, her family succeeded in obtaining a court order for the patient to get medication for her psychiatric illness. Which medication should this patient be given at this time?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol (Haldol) is an appropriate treatment for this psychotic patient[cite: 72]. Acute psychosis, with significant risk for impulsive behavior such as suicide attempts, is effectively treated with Haldol[cite: 73]. Imipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant, is lethal in overdose and should be prescribed carefully and not at all in high doses to actively suicidal patients[cite: 74]. In a patient with a history of substance abuse, benzodiazepines such as lorazepam should be carefully prescribed[cite: 75]. Benzodiazepines also work only by sedating without addressing this patient's psychosis[cite: 76]. Carbamazepine and lithium are mood stabilizers indicated for patients with bipolar disorder[cite: 77].

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old single male patient committed suicide while on a 4-hour therapeutic pass from the hospital before anticipated discharge. The patient was hospitalized with a diagnosis of major depression, single episode, and suicidal ideation. The patient steadfastly denied suicidal thoughts or impulses after admission. He experienced moderate to severe depression, anhedonia, global insomnia, hopelessness, agitation, and loss of appetite. The patient signed a suicide prevention contract, promising to inform the psychiatrist immediately of any suicidal ideation or impulses. After antidepressant treatment was started, the patient’s energy level improved. The man’s family sued the psychiatrist for wrongful death. The expert found no evidence in the psychiatric record that a formal suicide risk assessment was conducted before the pass was issued. During the trial, the psychiatrist testified that he did a formal suicide risk assessment but that it was an oversight that he did not record it. Which of the following is the most likely outcome of a trial under these circumstances?

options.text: The psychiatrist is not liable because a formal assessment of suicide risk was done.
The psychiatrist is not liable because adequate medical treatment was started.
The psychiatrist is not liable because the patient contracted for safety.
The psychiatrist is liable because a formal assessment of suicide risk was not documented.
The psychiatrist is liable because antidepressant therapy is known to increase the risk for suicide.

correct_answer.text: The psychiatrist is liable because a formal assessment of suicide risk was not documented.

correct_answers.text: The psychiatrist is liable because a formal assessment of suicide risk was not documented.

questions.explanation: The failure to adequately document events in the written clinical record is a major reason for lack of credibility to legal testimony[cite: 79]. The psychiatrist in this case testified that he completed a formal assessment of suicide risk, but there is no way to prove this is true with no documentation[cite: 80]. Although the patient was at a greater risk of suicide after administration of an antidepressant drug, the psychiatrist cannot be held liable for starting treatment with an antidepressant, which is the standard of care[cite: 81]. It is also arguable that the psychiatrist had not placed total reliance on the suicide prevention contract but had used it appropriately to assess the working alliance with the patient, that is, the patient's willingness to work toward getting better[cite: 82]. There is an adage in legal circles that if it is not documented, it was not done[cite: 83, 85].

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man has a documented history of paranoid schizophrenia. Upon returning home from work one day, he finds his wife in bed with another man. He immediately grabs a butcher knife and kills both his wife and her lover. He then systematically attempts to dispose of the bodies but is caught in the act. What is the most likely outcome of a trial using the M’Naghten rules under these circumstances?

options.text: Not guilty by reason of insanity
Not guilty by reason of diminished capacity

questions.explanation: To be found not guilty by reason of insanity, the defendant, as a result of a severe mental disease or defect, must be unable to appreciate the nature and quality or the wrongfulness of his acts[cite: 87]. In making an insanity determination, the threshold issue is not the existence of a mental disease or defect per se but the lack of substantial capacity caused by it[cite: 88]. In this case, the fact that the man tried to dispose of the bodies shows he was aware of the criminal act, negating any insanity plea[cite: 89]. For conviction of any crime, a criminal state of mind (mens rea) must be accompanied by the commission of a prohibited act (actus reus)[cite: 90]. Both must be present for a guilty verdict, and neither has to do with mental illness[cite: 91]. The physical act must be conscious and volitional for a person to be found guilty[cite: 92]. The law also recognizes shades of mental impairment that can affect mens rea, but not necessarily to the extent of completely nullifying it[cite: 93]. The concept of diminished capacity allows the defendant to introduce medical and psychological evidence that relates directly to the mens rea for the crime charged without having to assert a defense of insanity[cite: 94]. For example, in the crime of assault with the intent to kill, psychiatric testimony may be permitted to address whether the offender acted with the purpose of committing homicide at the time of the assault[cite: 95]. Mental illness per se is not a defense, and nothing in the case indicates this man did not intend to kill his wife and her lover[cite: 96].

questions.question_text: In the case above, which of the following is the most appropriate placement for this man?
questions.explanation: What happens to a defendant after a judge or jury returns a finding of insanity depends on the crime committed and on the state in which the trial takes place[cite: 98]. Usually, those found "not guilty by reason of insanity" are confined for treatment in a special hospital for severely mentally ill persons who have committed crimes[cite: 99]. After a period of time, the person may request a hearing to determine if he or she is no longer a danger to him- or herself or others or is no longer mentally ill and is therefore eligible to be released[cite: 100]. Studies show that persons found not guilty by reason of insanity, on average, are held at least as long as and often longer than persons found guilty and sent to prison for similar crimes[cite: 101]. In this case, the person was sent to jail because his insanity defense did not prevail[cite: 102]. Jails are correctional facilities that confine individuals involved in the criminal justice system who are awaiting trial or serving short sentences for misdemeanors[cite: 103]. A local lockup may be a police precinct cell, a sheriff's office, or any other place, including a correctional facility used to detain an arrested individual pending arraignment[cite: 104].

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old mentally retarded woman is arrested for killing her mother. At her trial, neither the defense nor the prosecution puts the woman on the stand because her communication skills are poor, and she is never fully evaluated by a psychiatrist before or during the trial. She is found guilty of murdering her mother and is sent to prison. Her father, although devastated, tells a lawyer his daughter is severely mentally retarded and cannot possibly be held responsible for the murder. Which of the following is the lawyer most likely to claim to appeal the decision?
questions.explanation: A writ of habeas corpus (literally, "you must have the body") is a legal procedure that asks a court to decide whether a patient has been hospitalized or imprisoned without due process of law[cite: 106]. The writ tests only whether a prisoner has been accorded due process, not whether he or she is guilty[cite: 107]. The automatism (or unconscious) defense recognizes that some criminal acts may be committed involuntarily[cite: 108]. Testimonial privilege is the right of the patient to maintain secrecy or confidentiality in the face of a subpoena[cite: 108, 110]. Parens patriae is the doctrine that allows the state to intervene and act as a surrogate for those who are unable to care for themselves or may harm themselves[cite: 111]. Respondeat superior is Latin for "let the master answer for the deed of the servant." [cite: 112] This states a person high in the chain of command is responsible for the actions of those under his or her supervision[cite: 113].

questions.question_text: If a patient threatens to harm another person,

options.text: psychiatrists in all states are required by law to perform some intervention to prevent the harm from occurring
psychiatrists in all states are permitted by law to perform some intervention to prevent the harm from occurring
the duty to protect patients and endangered third parties should be considered a professional obligation and only secondarily a legal issue
the Tarasoff duty applies only in state in which there is a duty to warn and to protect
psychiatrists cannot intervene as they must protect the confidentiality privilege

correct_answer.text: the duty to protect patients and endangered third parties should be considered a professional obligation and only secondarily a legal issue

correct_answers.text: the duty to protect patients and endangered third parties should be considered a professional obligation and only secondarily a legal issue

questions.explanation: The duty to protect patients and endangered third parties should be considered primarily a professional and moral obligation and only secondarily a legal duty[cite: 115]. Most psychiatrists acted to protect their patients and threatened others from violence long before Tarasoff[cite: 116]. Psychiatrists should consider the Tarasoff duty to be a national standard of care even if they practice in states that do not have a duty to warn and protect[cite: 117]. Indeed, not all states have duty to warn statutes, so there is no legal obligation necessarily in all states that permits or requires psychiatrists to prevent the harm from occurring[cite: 118]. If a patient gives the psychiatrist sufficient reason to believe that a warning should be issued to an endangered third party, the confidentiality of the communication that gave rise to the warning may be lost[cite: 119].

questions.question_text: Incompetence

options.text: is a global assessment of mental function
can be presumed if a patient is psychiatrically institutionalized
is rendered by virtue of a patient having a mental disability

questions.explanation: Incompetence is a broad concept that encompasses many different legal issues and contexts[cite: 121]. It refers to a court adjudication[cite: 122]. Incapacity indicates a functional inability determined by a clinician[cite: 122]. It is a legal term that is applied to people who are considered by law not to be mentally capable of performing a particular act or assuming a particular role[cite: 123]. Its adjudication is issue specific; someone judged to be incompetent to do one thing is not automatically incompetent to do other things[cite: 124]. A lack of competency cannot be presumed from a person's treatment for mental illness or from institutionalization[cite: 125]. Mental disability does not necessarily render a person incompetent or incompetent in all areas of functioning[cite: 126].

questions.question_text: A tort is a
questions.explanation: A tort is any wrongdoing for which an action for damages may be brought[cite: 128]. A writ is a written court order directing a person to perform or refrain from performing a specific act[cite: 129]. A subpoena is a writ commanding a designated person upon whom it has been served to appear (as in court or before a congressional committee) under a penalty (as a charge of contempt) for failure to comply[cite: 130]. A judgment is a formal decision or determination on a matter or case by a court[cite: 131]. A good deed is obviously not a tort[cite: 132].

questions.question_text: An example of a tort is when a doctor

options.text: dates a family member of a former patient
tells a patient that sex with him or her is therapeutic
maintains confidentiality in the face of a subpoena
lists the adverse effects of drugs when prescribing

correct_answer.text: tells a patient that sex with him or her is therapeutic

correct_answers.text: tells a patient that sex with him or her is therapeutic

questions.explanation: In a tort, wrongdoers are motivated by the intent to harm another person or should have realized that such harm is likely to result from their actions[cite: 134]. For example, telling a patient that sex with the therapist is therapeutic perpetrates a fraud[cite: 135]. Although hugging a patient and dating a patient's family member are both unethical, they are examples of boundary violations, not a tort[cite: 136]. Various criminal law statutes have been used against psychiatrists who violate this ethical principle[cite: 137]. Privilege is the right to maintain confidentiality in the face of a subpoena[cite: 138]. Privileged communications are statements made by certain persons within a relationship such as husband-wife, priest-penitent, or doctor-patient that the law protects from forced disclosure on the witness stand[cite: 138, 139]. Listing the adverse effects of drugs when prescribing drugs is an example of good medical practice and is not a tort[cite: 140].

questions.question_text: Psychiatrists can be sued for
questions.explanation: Psychiatrists, similar to other people, can be sued for anything[cite: 142]. This includes battery, defined as the unlawful and unwanted touching or striking of one person by another with the intention of bringing about a harmful or offensive contact[cite: 143]. Invasion of privacy, defined as the intrusion into the personal life of another without just cause, can give the person whose privacy has been invaded a right to bring a lawsuit for damages against the person or entity that intruded[cite: 144]. Misrepresentation, defined as a statement made by a party to a contract, that a thing relating to it is in fact in a particular way when he or she knows it is not so[cite: 145]. False imprisonment, defined as restraining another person without having the legal right to do so, is a misdemeanor and a tort[cite: 146].

questions.question_text: The most frequent issue involving lawsuits against psychiatrists is
questions.explanation: Suicide and suicide attempts are the most frequent causes for lawsuits against psychiatrists; 50 percent of suicides lead to malpractice actions by relatives[cite: 148, 149]. The greatest degree of supervision (inpatient setting) is associated with the most culpability[cite: 150]. The use of restraints, drug reactions, and patients committing violence are all potential causes of malpractice that can be forestalled with proper documentation of clinical decision making and informed consent[cite: 151]. Sexual involvement with a patient is both illegal and unethical[cite: 152].

questions.question_text: Durable Power of Attorney

options.text: is an attorney whose main expertise is psychiatric malpractice cases
is power that permits patients to have visitation rights
is a document that permits the doctor to breach confidentiality
is a document that permits persons to make provisions for their decision-making capacity
has a limited duration of time

correct_answer.text: is a document that permits persons to make provisions for their decision-making capacity

correct_answers.text: is a document that permits persons to make provisions for their decision-making capacity

questions.explanation: A modern development that permits persons to make provisions for their own anticipated loss of decision-making capacity is called a durable power of attorney[cite: 153]. The document permits the advance selection of a substitute decision maker who can act without the necessity of court proceedings when the signatory becomes incompetent through illness, progressive dementia, or perhaps a relapse of bipolar I disorder[cite: 154]. The term durable means that it continues forever and does not have a limited duration of time[cite: 155].

questions.question_text: Involuntary termination of treatment of a patient by a therapist

options.text: may result in a malpractice claim of abandonment
cannot be done during a patient emergency
should include transfer of services to others

questions.explanation: A potential pitfall of involuntary discharge or termination is the charge of abandonment[cite: 156]. Malpractice litigation is often associated with situations in which there are bad feelings and a bad outcome[cite: 157]. Consultation and careful documentation are important safeguards[cite: 158]. Charges of abandonment can be avoided by referring the patient to another hospital or therapist[cite: 158]. Some authorities recommend giving a patient three names of therapists, clinics, or hospitals[cite: 158, 159]. A patient's treatment cannot be terminated while in a state of emergency[cite: 160]. The emergency must be resolved (e.g.. by hospitalization in cases of dangerousness) before treatment can be terminated and the patient transferred[cite: 161].

questions.question_text: A person considered competent to be executed

options.text: must be aware of the punishment
may come to whatever peace is appropriate with religious beliefs
might recall forgotten details of the events

questions.explanation: The requirement for competence to be executed rests on a few general principles[cite: 163]. A person's awareness of what is happening is supposed to heighten the retributive element of the punishment[cite: 164, 165]. Punishment is meaningless unless the person is aware of it and knows the punishment's purpose[cite: 165]. A competent person who is about to be executed is believed to be in the best position to make whatever peace is appropriate with religious beliefs, including confession and absolution[cite: 166]. A competent person who is about to be executed preserves, until the end, the possibility (admittedly slight) of recalling a forgotten detail of the events or the crime that may prove exonerating[cite: 167].

questions.question_text: Pick the best answer regarding Dusky v United States.

options.text: Harmless mental patients cannot be confined against their wills without treatment if they can survive outside.
An involuntary patient who is not receiving treatment has a constitutional right to be discharged.
A test of competence was approved to see if a criminal defendant can rationally consult with a lawyer and has a factual (and rational) understanding of the proceedings against him or her.
Civilly committed persons have a constitutional right to adequate treatment.
A clinician must notify the intended victim(s) when there is an imminent threat posed by his or her patient.

correct_answer.text: A test of competence was approved to see if a criminal defendant can rationally consult with a lawyer and has a factual (and rational) understanding of the proceedings against him or her.

correct_answers.text: A test of competence was approved to see if a criminal defendant can rationally consult with a lawyer and has a factual (and rational) understanding of the proceedings against him or her.

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court, in Dusky v United States (1960), approved a test of competence that seeks to ascertain whether a criminal defendant "has sufficient present ability to consult with his lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and whether he has a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings against him." [cite: 169] In the 1976 case of O'Connor v Donaldson, the Supreme Court ruled that harmless mental patients cannot be confined against their wills without treatment if they can survive outside[cite: 170]. In 1966, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals ruled in Rouse v Cameron that an involuntary inpatient who is not receiving treatment has a constitutional right to be discharged[cite: 171]. According to this decision, the purpose of involuntary hospitalization is treatment[cite: 172]. In Wyatt v Stickney (1971), it was decided that civilly committed patients have a constitutional right to receive adequate treatment[cite: 173]. In Tarasoff I (the case of Tarasoff v Regents of the University of California in 1974), it was ruled that a psychotherapist or physician who has reason to believe that a patient may injure or kill someone must notify the potential victim, the patient's relatives or friends, or the authorities[cite: 174].

questions.question_text: In a child custody dispute, which of the following is not true?

options.text: A natural parent has the inherent right to be named custodial parent.
The best interest of the mother may be served by naming her as the custodial parent.
More fathers are asserting custodial claims.
Courts presume that a child is best served by maternal custody when the mother is a good and fit parent.
In 5 percent of all cases, fathers are named the custodians.

correct_answer.text: A natural parent has the inherent right to be named custodial parent.

correct_answers.text: A natural parent has the inherent right to be named custodial parent.

questions.explanation: The action of a court in a child custody dispute is now predicated on the child's best interests[cite: 176]. The maxim reflects the idea that a natural parent does not have an inherent right to be named a custodial parent, but the presumption, although a bit eroded, remains in favor of the mother in the case of young children[cite: 177]. As a rule, courts presume that the welfare of a child of tender years generally is best served by maternal custody when the mother is a good and fit parent[cite: 178]. The best interest of the mother may be served by naming her as the custodial parent because a mother may never resolve the effects of the loss of a child, but her best interest is not to be equated ipso facto with the best interest of the child[cite: 179]. More fathers are asserting custodial claims[cite: 180]. In about 5 percent of all cases, fathers are named custodians[cite: 180]. The movement supporting women's rights is also enhancing the chances of paternal custody[cite: 181]. With more women going to work outside the home, the traditional rationale for maternal custody has less force today than it did in the past[cite: 182].

questions.question_text: Confidential communications can be shared with which of the following without the patient’s consent?
questions.explanation: Confidentiality pertains to the premise that all information imparted to a physician by a patient should be held secret[cite: 184]. However, sharing information with other staff members treating the patient, clinical supervisors, and a medical or psychiatric consultant does not require the patient's permission[cite: 185]. Sharing patient information with the patient's family, the patient's attorney, the patient's previous therapist, or an insurer of the patient does require the patient's permission[cite: 186, 188]. Courts may compel disclosure of confidential material (subpoena duces tecum)[cite: 189]. In emergencies, limited information may be released, but after the emergency, the clinician should inform the patient[cite: 190].

questions.question_text: Product rule is concerned with
questions.explanation: In 1954, in the case of Durham v United States, a decision was made by Judge David Bazelon, a pioneering jurist in forensic psychiatry in the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, that resulted in the product rule of criminal responsibility[cite: 192]. An accused is not criminally responsible if his or her unlawful act was the product of mental disease or defect[cite: 193]. Judge Bazelon stated that the purpose of the rule was to get good and complete psychiatric testimony[cite: 194]. He sought to break the criminal law out of the theoretical straitjacket of the M'Naghten test[cite: 195]. Testimonial privilege is the right to maintain secrecy or confidentiality in the face of a subpoena[cite: 196]. The privilege belongs to the patient, not to the physician, and it is waivable by the patient[cite: 197]. Involuntary admission involves the question of whether the patient is a danger to him or herself or others, such as in the suicidal or homicidal patient[cite: 198]. Because these individuals do not recognize their need for hospital care, application for admission to a hospital may be made by a relative or friend and is involuntary[cite: 199]. Competency to stand trial refers to defendants being able to comprehend the nature and the object of the proceedings against them so they can consult with counsel and assist in preparing the defense[cite: 200].

questions.question_text: Negligent prescription practices may include
questions.explanation: Negligent prescription practices usually include exceeding recommended dosages and then failing to adjust the medication level to therapeutic levels, unreasonable mixing of drugs, prescribing medication that is not indicated, prescribing too many drugs at one time, and then failing to disclose medication effects[cite: 202]. Although exceeding the recommended dosage may be considered negligent, if it must be done, it should be documented in the patient's chart[cite: 203]. Multiple psychotropic medications must be prescribed with special care because of their possible harmful interactions and adverse effects[cite: 204]. Psychiatrists must explain the diagnosis, risks, and benefits of the drug[cite: 205]. Informed consent should be obtained each time a medication is changed and a new drug is introduced[cite: 206]. If patients are injured because they were not properly informed of the risks and consequences of taking a medication, sufficient grounds may exist for a malpractice action[cite: 207]. Finally, poor handwriting and the misreading of the prescription by nurses or pharmacists is a major source of error[cite: 208].

questions.question_text: The Gault decision applies to
questions.explanation: The Gault decision applies to minors, those under the care of a parent or guardian and usually younger than 18 years of age[cite: 210]. In the case of minors, the parent or guardian is the person legally empowered to give consent to medical treatment[cite: 211]. However, most states by statute list specific diseases or conditions that a minor may consent to have treated, such as sexually transmitted infections, pregnancy, substance-related disorders, and contagious diseases[cite: 212, 214]. In an emergency, a physician may treat a minor without parental consent[cite: 214]. The trend is to adopt the mature minor rule, allowing minors to consent to treatment under ordinary circumstances[cite: 215]. As a result of the Gault decision, the juvenile must now be represented by counsel, be able to confront witnesses, and be given proper notice of any charges[cite: 216]. Emancipated minors have the rights of adults when it can be demonstrated that they are living as adults with control over their own lives[cite: 217]. A writ of habeas corpus may be proclaimed on behalf of anyone who claims he or she is being deprived of liberty illegally[cite: 218]. The legal procedure asks a court to decide whether hospitalization has been accomplished without due process of the law, and the petition must be heard by a court at once, regardless of the manner or form in which it is filed[cite: 219]. Hospitals are obligated to submit these petitions to the court immediately[cite: 220]. Informed consent is knowledge of the risks and alternatives of a treatment method and formal acceptance of treatment[cite: 221]. Under classical tort (a tort is a wrongful act) theory, an intentional touching to which one has given no consent is a battery[cite: 222]. Thus, the administration of electroconvulsive therapy or chemotherapy, although it may be therapeutic, is battery when done without consent[cite: 223]. Indeed, any unauthorized touching outside of conventional social intercourse constitutes a battery[cite: 224]. It is an offense to the dignity of the person, an invasion of the right of self-determination, for which punitive and actual damages may be imposed[cite: 225].

questions.question_text: Situations in which there is an obligation on the part of the physician to report to authorities information that may be confidential include

options.text: the case of a patient who will probably commit murder and can only be stopped by notification of police
the case of a patient who will probably commit suicide and can only be stopped by notification of police
the case of a patient who has potentially life-threatening responsibilities (e.g., airline pilot) and who shows marked impairment of judgment

questions.explanation: In some situations-such as suspected child abuse the physician must report to the authorities, as specifically required by law[cite: 227]. According to the American Psychiatric Association, confidentiality may be broken when the patient will probably commit murder and the act can only be stopped by notification of police, when the patient will probably commit suicide and the act can only be stopped by notification of police, or when a patient who has potentially life-threatening responsibilities (e.g., an airline pilot) shows marked impairment of judgment[cite: 228].

questions.question_text: Patient voluntarily requests
questions.explanation: Most states have enacted statutes that regulate the use of restraints, often specifying the circumstances in which restraints can be used usually when a risk of harm to self or danger to others is imminent[cite: 234]. Statutory regulation of the use of seclusion is much less common[cite: 235]. About half of states have laws governing seclusion[cite: 235]. Most states with laws regarding seclusion and restraint require some type of documentation of the usage[cite: 236]. A number of courts and state statutes outline certain due process procedures that must be followed before restraint or seclusion can be used for nonclinically indicated, disciplinary purposes[cite: 237]. These include some form of notice, a hearing, and involvement of an impartial decision maker[cite: 238, 245]. The American Psychiatric Association Task Force on the Psychiatric Uses of Seclusion and Restraint has developed guidelines for the appropriate use of seclusion and restraints, and The Joint Commission (formerly the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations [JCAHO]) has promulgated guidelines for hospitals regarding seclusion and restraint requirements[cite: 246]. Professional opinion concerning the clinical uses of physical restraints and seclusion varies considerably among psychiatrists[cite: 247]. Seclusion can be justified on both clinical and legal grounds for a variety of uses unless precluded by state freedom from restraint and seclusion statutes[cite: 248]. Seclusion and restraint raise complex psychiatric legal issues and have both indications and contraindications (Tables 57.1 and 57.2)[cite: 249]. Furthermore, seclusion and restraint have become increasingly regulated over the past decade[cite: 250]. Legal challenges to the use of restraints and seclusion have been brought on behalf of institutionalized mentally ill and mentally retarded persons[cite: 251]. Typically, these lawsuits do not stand alone but are part of a challenge to a wide range of alleged abuses[cite: 252]. Generally, courts hold or consent decrees provide that restraints and seclusion can be implemented only when a patient creates a risk of harm to him or herself or others and no less restrictive alternative is available[cite: 253]. Additional restrictions include the following: 1. Restraint and seclusion can only be implemented by a written order from an appropriate medical official[cite: 254, 255]. 2. Orders are to be confined to specific, time-limited periods[cite: 256]. 3. A patient's condition must be reviewed regularly and documented[cite: 257]. 4. Any extension of an original order must be reviewed and reauthorized[cite: 258].

questions.question_text: Known commonly as the right–wrong test
questions.explanation: The precedent for determining legal responsibility was established in the British courts in 1843[cite: 268]. The M'Naghten rule is known commonly as the right-wrong test because the alleged perpetrator is not guilty by reason of insanity if he or she is unable to tell right from wrong because of a mental disease[cite: 268]. In 1922, jurists in England reexamined the M'Naghten rule and suggested broadening the concept of insanity in criminal cases to include the concept of the irresistible impulse that is, a person charged with a criminal offense is not responsible for an act if the act was committed under circumstances that the person was unable to resist because of mental disease[cite: 269]. To most psychiatrists, the law is unsatisfactory because it covers only a small group of those who are mentally ill[cite: 270]. However, it was used successfully in Virginia in the 1994 case of Virginia v Bobbitt in which the defendant was acquitted of malicious wounding[cite: 271]. The wife had cut off her husband's penis after apparently enduring a prolonged period of sexual, physical, and emotional abuse[cite: 272]. In 1954 in the case of Durham v United States, a decision resulted in the product rule of criminal responsibility, or the Durham rule, which states that an accused is not criminally responsible if his or her unlawful act was the product of mental disease or mental defect[cite: 273]. Judge Bazelon stated that the purpose of the rule was to get good and complete psychiatric testimony[cite: 274]. In 1972, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia in United States v Brawner discarded the rule in favor of the American Law Institute's (ALI's) 1962 model penal code test of criminal responsibility[cite: 275]. In its model penal code, the ALI recommended the following test of criminal responsibility: (1) persons are not responsible for criminal conduct if at the time of such conduct, as the result of mental disease or defect, they lacked substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality of their conduct or to conform their conduct to the requirement of the law, and (2) the term "mental disease or defect" in this test does not include an abnormality manifested only by repeated criminal or otherwise antisocial conduct[cite: 276, 278]. Other attempts at reform have included the defense of diminished capacity, which is based on the claim that the defendant experienced some impairment (usually but not always because of mental illness) sufficient to interfere with the ability to formulate a specific element of the particular crime charged[cite: 279]. Hence, the defense finds its most common use with so-called specific-intent crimes, such as first-degree murder[cite: 280].

questions.question_text: Harmless mental patients cannot be confined against their will.
questions.explanation: Various landmark legal cases have affected psychiatry and the law over the years[cite: 287]. In the 1976 case of O'Connor v Donaldson, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that harmless mental patients cannot be confined against their will without treatment if they can survive outside[cite: 288]. According to the Court, a finding of mental illness alone cannot justify a state's confining persons in a hospital against their will; such patients must be considered dangerous to themselves or others before they are confined[cite: 289, 290]. In 1971, in Wyatt v Stickney in Alabama Federal District Court, it was decided that persons civilly committed to a mental institution have a constitutional right to receive adequate care [cite: 291]. and standards were established for staffing, nutrition, physical facilities, and treatment[cite: 292]. In 1966, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals in Rouse v Cameron ruled that the purpose of involuntary hospitalization is treatment and that a patient who is not receiving treatment has a constitutional right to be discharged from the hospital[cite: 293]. In The Myth of Mental Illness, Thomas Szasz argued that the various psychiatric diagnoses are totally devoid of significance and that therefore all forced confinements because of mental illness are unjust[cite: 294]. Szasz contended that psychiatrists have no place in the courts of law[cite: 295].
